title: Higher Education and Funding: Threat of Insolvency and International Students
text:
Higher Education and Funding: Threat of Insolvency and International Students

# Higher Education and Funding: Threat of Insolvency and International Students

This is a House of Commons committee report, with recommendations to government. The Government has two months to respond.

## Ninth Report of Session 2024–26

Author: Education Committee

Date Published: Tuesday 12 May 2026

## Summary

### Student Report: Universities at Breaking Point

The higher education sector in England is facing a financial crisis that now poses a real risk of institutional insolvency. We heard compelling evidence that, without urgent and coordinated action, there is a clear possibility of a university closing. The consequences would be severe, not only for students and staff, but for local economies, communities and the UK’s global academic reputation.

Throughout our inquiry, witnesses underlined the immense value of higher education institutions. Universities are major economic drivers, creating skilled jobs and sustaining local economies through student and staff spending. During our visit to the University of Warwick, we saw at first-hand how universities incubate startups, support innovation and help develop the next generation of entrepreneurs. Research based in universities has delivered recognised national and global benefits, including the rapid development of COVID-19 vaccines. Universities also act as anchor institutions: in many areas they are among the largest employers, train public-sector workers, support local businesses through research partnerships, and work with schools to raise attainment. They are indispensable to the delivery of the Government’s Missions.

In this report, we recommend that the Government fully recognise and reflect the economic and civic anchor role of universities when developing policy and responding to financial distress in the sector.

### Mounting financial pressures

The financial foundations of higher education have been steadily eroded. The freezing of UK undergraduate tuition fees in cash terms for most of the past fifteen years has resulted in sustained realterms cuts to the core funding of universities. While we welcome the Government’s commitment to allow fees to rise in line with forecast inflation from September 2025, this makes it crucial that inflation forecasts, previously prone to underestimating actual inflation, are robust and accurate.

As a result of the fee freeze, universities have been driven to increase income from fees for postgraduate and international students, creating an unhealthy reliance on international recruitment to crosssubsidise both teaching and research. Many providers have also expanded franchising and transnational education provision, with too many exposing themselves to additional financial and reputational risk. At the same time, government research funding has consistently failed to meet the promised 80% of full economic cost. Universities are also facing rising costs due to inflation, regulatory burdens, higher employer National Insurance contributions, and for post-1992 institutions increased contributions to the Teachers’ Pension Scheme.

Many universities have taken on commercial debt, leaving them exposed to higher interest rates and restrictive borrowing covenants. Weaknesses in institutional governance at some HE institutions have compounded these challenges. Taken together, these pressures have led the Office for Students to warn that 45% of higher education providers could run a deficit in the 2025–26 financial year without mitigating action. Across the country, universities are already responding by closing courses and campuses and making staff redundant.

We are calling on the Government to confirm its commitment to funding research at 80% of full economic cost and to undertake a review of the longterm sustainability of research funding. We also recommend that the Government works with the sector to address sharply rising pension costs without undermining staff pensions.

### Regulation, governance and early warning

We are calling on the Office for Students to review the cumulative cost of regulation, issue clear guidance to institutions seeking to exit or scale back franchising arrangements and develop a sectorwide governance improvement programme. This could include measures such as deferring senior leaders’ performancerelated pay until after they leave office.

Given universities’ anchor role in their local communities, the collapse of a provider would be calamitous. It would risk closing off opportunities for students from lower socio-economic backgrounds, lead to the loss of irreplaceable expertise, and undermine local research and development. The ripple effects would be felt throughout local economies and internationally.

In this report, we recommend that the Government urgently establish a formal earlywarning and intervention protocol, triggered when the Office for Students categorises an institution as at risk of insolvency. This protocol should set out clearly when government intervention is warranted and provide a menu of responses, ranging from restructuring to an orderly exit.

### Insolvency, intervention and student protection

We heard deeply conflicting evidence about what would happen if a university, particularly a Higher Education Corporation or a Royal Charter body, became insolvent. While the Government contends that such institutions could enter liquidation and continue operating, legal specialists and other stakeholders told us liquidation would require immediate cessation of trading.

We are calling on the Government to legislate to clarify the legal position and to set out transparent criteria for intervention across the different legal forms of higher education providers.

We also examined whether the sector needs a bespoke higher education insolvency regime. We conclude that it does. Such a regime should build on lessons from the further education sector and prioritise student teachout, protection of strategically critical courses and avoidance of geographical “cold-spots”. We were concerned by the Office for Students’ admission that current Student Protection Plans would not be sufficient in the event of a large provider collapse.

We therefore recommend that student protection regulations be significantly strengthened and expanded to protect not only students, but staff and local communities.

### Collaboration, cold-spots and skills

We considered alternatives to insolvency, including mergers, greater collaboration and shared services. While mergers have a role to play, they are no panacea. Barriers including VAT rules and competition law currently deter collaboration.

We are calling on the Government to review VAT treatment that prevents the sharing of backoffice services and to work with the Competition and Markets Authority to ensure competition law does not inhibit productive collaborations.

We are also concerned about the growing risk of geographic and subjectbased “cold-spots”, affecting areas and disciplines such as chemistry, music and modern languages. These trends reflect an absence of strategic oversight of regional higher education provision.

In this report, we recommend stronger coordination between universities, further education colleges, combined authorities, metro mayors, local authorities and government departments, including the Office for Students and UK Research and Innovation. We also call on the Government to reform the Strategic Priorities Grant to better support highcost and strategically vital subjects and prevent cold-spots emerging.

### International students and immigration policy

The sector’s reliance on international students is a direct consequence of government funding decisions. Given this, we are calling on the Government to consider immigration policy and higher education sustainability in a joined up way. If Ministers want to reduce international student numbers, they must set out how they will maintain the financial viability of universities.

We recommend that the Home Office becomes a co-owner of the International Education Strategy and is required to align immigration policy with it.

The Government has recently announced policies expected to reduce international student numbers, including shortening poststudy work visas and tightening Basic Compliance Assessment requirements. These changes come amid intensifying global competition and an expected medium term decline in demand from China.

We welcome the Government’s decision to rejoin Erasmus+ from 2027 and call for clarity on its implications, alongside lessons learned from the Turing Scheme. We also recommend that the Government monitors the impact of immigration changes closely, reviews graduate visa reforms after 18 months, and ensures data underpinning BCA changes support diversification rather than constrain it.

### International student levy

We heard strong concerns about the proposed £925 per student international levy, due to be introduced from 2028, which would fund targeted maintenance grants. Providers warned they may be unable to absorb or pass on the cost and that the levy could disproportionately hit institutions serving local and disadvantaged communities.

We welcome the reintroduction of maintenance grants, but we are calling on the Government to publish full details of the levy’s costs, distributional impact and interaction with existing maintenance loans and the Lifelong Learning Entitlement. We also recommend that the Government engages meaningfully with the sector on price sensitivity among international students and confirms whether levy revenue will fund other skills priorities.

Without decisive action, the financial crisis facing higher education risks undermining students’ life chances, hollowing out regional economies and damaging one of the UK’s most valuable national assets.

## Introduction

### The crisis facing higher education

1. The higher education sector is facing a financial crisis. The higher education regulator in England, the Office for Students, told us that it fears 24 providers, including seven with over 3,000 students, are at risk of insolvency and market exit in the next twelve months. 1 While no university has ever closed in England due to insolvency, 2 the risk is clear. It could have a catastrophic impact, not only on the students and staff connected with the institution, but on the wider local economy and community.

### Our inquiry

2. Our inquiry focused on the threat of insolvency and international students. The two are closely interconnected given the importance of income from international students’ fees to fund many higher education providers.

3. We are also conscious of the diverse nature of the higher education sector. There are universities of different size and scale, some singularly focused on a particular area, others multi-faculty. Higher education is also extensively provided by colleges, and by private providers. Specialist provision in subjects such as music, drama and dance is provided by world-famous schools and conservatoires.

4. The financial difficulties facing the higher education sector were already apparent when we held a pre-appointment hearing on 4 March 2025 with Professor Edward Peck, the Government’s preferred candidate to be Chair of the Office for Students. 3 We also held an one-off deep dive session with higher education sector stakeholders on 8 April 2025, following which we wrote to the Secretary of State highlighting the many issues that were raised with us. 4 We launched this inquiry on 12 June 2025. 5 

5. We have published ninety-nine pieces of written evidence and held two oral evidence sessions. In the first session we heard from witnesses focused on the threat of insolvency, and on international students respectively.
